ISE 754: Logistics Engineering, Fall 2026

With stationary data and symmetric loss, mean or median suffice; with asymmetry, trends, or added information, optimization within a regression framework is required.

No new Julia packages used.

## 1. Roles of inventory

Lecture 3.3 classified inventory by its role and its position in the materials flow (Table 1 in Lecture 3.3) and then dealt only with economic stock, the cycle stock of truck shipments. All three roles are taken up here in turn: working stock, economic stock and safety stock.

Three things make production system design hard. First, things are not always where they are wanted when they are wanted, which requires working stock: it takes time, and time is money. Second, resources are lumpy, which calls for economic stock: more can be cheaper. Third, things vary, and variability can be known or unknown. Uncertainty or randomness is unknown variability, and it is what requires safety stock: a little extra just in case can save a lot later.

Each of the three types of inventory answers one of these difficulties. That things are not always where they are wanted when they are wanted is obvious, but what it implies is the concept of working stock. Working stock is not a big issue in trucking, but in international supply by ocean transport the whole game is essentially working stock: things take time, and time is money. The reason for economic stock is that a lot of resources are lumpy. A truckload costs about the same whether it carries one pallet or is filled to its maximum payload: fuel economy is a little lower with a full load, but the biggest costs, the driver and the vehicle itself, are almost independent of how much is put on it, so it is all or nothing. In periodic truck transport, Lecture 3.3, that gave rise to the problem of determining how much to ship, solved by a square-root formula for a truckload and numerically for less than truckload: the best trade-off between incurring the transport cost and carrying the inventory, since shipping more means more inventory but less transport. Economic stock is that sweet spot. The third type has to do with the fact that things vary, and the important distinction, which can seem strange at first, is that variability can be either known or unknown. Variability is usually equated with uncertainty or randomness, as if the words meant the same thing, but here the two have to be distinguished. The biggest impact of known variability on a production system comes from batching, such as transporting an entire truckload: just before a store receives a truckload it might have nothing in stock, and when the truck arrives its warehouse is filled to the ceiling. So with any batching, even when everything is perfectly constant, the inventory level goes from zero up to some high level and back down again. That can be known exactly and still make the system difficult to operate, just because the level is changing. The more common type is unknown variability, also called uncertainty or randomness, and it is what requires safety stock: a little extra just in case can save a lot later. It is only because of unknown variability that safety stock is needed; otherwise the system could be planned exactly.

Working stock is the stock needed to operate a business. A product purchased in Shanghai and transported to the United States spends two or three weeks on a ship, inventory that has to be paid for although it is doing nothing except being transported: from a finance point of view, \$1 million of inventory bought in Shanghai that takes three weeks to arrive has to be financed for three weeks before the product can be sold. A store is the same: it has to purchase the items on its shelves, and if they sit there for days or weeks before customers buy them, that is the store’s working inventory. Economic stock is the general term for inventory that comes from resources being lumpy, and the lumpiness the course has dealt with most is the truck driver: because a truck has a human driver, the truck is made as large as possible and shipped full whenever possible. The optimal shipment size of periodic truck shipments, Lecture 3.3, traded the inventory cost against the transport cost, since a large shipment cannot be consumed immediately and is consumed over time instead, so the larger the shipment, the more the inventory but the lower the transport cost. The square-root formula that gave that size determined a type of economic stock called cycle stock. Safety stock is the most complicated type, and it is not directly the fact that things vary that makes it necessary, since variability can be known. A seasonal product might see a 50% increase in demand every fall, almost deterministically from one season to the next; there is no real randomness in that, and it can be handled with other types of inventory and deterministic techniques. The variability that requires safety stock is randomness or uncertainty, unknown variability, and in a perfect world safety stock would never be needed.

The whole course so far can be characterized as the interplay between two of these difficulties. Not having things where they are wanted when they are wanted is the whole motivation for logistics and transportation, but by itself it does not lead to much of interest. What makes the problems interesting is its combination with the fact that resources are lumpy. In the uncapacitated facility location (UFL) problem of Lecture 2.4, a fixed cost is why there is not a new facility at every location, and economizing on it means having fewer. In freight transport, packages are not each shipped on their own little vehicle but together on a 53-ft truck carrying 25 tons, because the driver is a lumpy resource, the ultimate lumpy resource, and one driver can take every pallet on the truck down the interstate. Much of the U.S. logistics network, especially for big-box retailers, can be viewed as designed so that everything ships full truckload, from the suppliers and to the stores, to reduce the lumpiness of the supply chain. Production inventory is the same: to economize on a setup cost, a plan is willing to carry inventory from one period to another, since a setup is another lumpy activity. And in routing, point-to-point deliveries are not cost effective, since a delivery vehicle cannot be scaled down to the size of a single package, so the packages are lumped together into one vehicle and routed. Variability has been deliberately kept off the table, since location, transport and routing problems are complicated enough without it. One-time safety stock is a simple way to bring it in, with the lumpiness and everything else pushed to the side, so that variability comes front and center.

The same units of inventory can serve multiple roles at each position in a production process. Working stock is held as part of the production process, and is also called in-process, pipeline, in-transit, or presentation stock. Economic stock is held to allow cheaper production, as cycle or anticipation stock. Safety stock is held to buffer the effects of uncertainty, as decoupling or MRO stock (maintenance, repair, and operations). Table 1 repeats Lecture 3.3’s classification of inventory by role and position.

Table 1: Inventory by role and position: why each role is held, and what it is at each position in the materials flow, from raw material through work in process to finished goods.

| Role | Why it is held | Position | What it is there |
|---|---|---|---|
| Working stock | to allow production, including transport | Raw material | in transit from supplier |
| | | Work in process | queuing between operations |
| | | Finished goods | in transit to customers, or presentation stock |
| Economic stock | to make purchasing or production cheaper | Raw material | cycle stock from truckloads |
| | | Work in process | batches spreading setup cost |
| | | Finished goods | seasonal pre-build |
| Safety stock | to buffer uncertainty | Raw material | buffer against supplier delay |
| | | Work in process | buffer between operations |
| | | Finished goods | buffer against uncertain demand |

In-process, pipeline, in-transit and presentation stock are all different terms for what is more generically working stock. Production here includes transportation as a type of production, whose product is the transportation itself. The truck shipments of Lecture 3.3 determined what is called cycle stock, and there is also what is called anticipation stock; both are economic stock. Safety stock, held to buffer against uncertainty, is covered in more depth in Sec. 4 and, for periodic safety stock, in Lecture 6.2.

Total logistics costs are any of the relevant costs associated with providing a logistics service, where a relevant cost is a cost that differs when comparing multiple alternatives and, as such, can be used in making a decision between the alternatives. Total logistics cost decomposes into three such terms, and its inventory cost into one term for each role that inventory plays:

$$
\hphantom{\underset{\displaystyle IC}{TLC}}\mathllap{TLC} = \mathrlap{TC + IC + PC}\hphantom{\underset{\displaystyle IC_\text{working} + IC_\text{economic} + IC_\text{safety}}{TC + IC + PC}} \tag{1}
$$

$$
\hphantom{\underset{\displaystyle IC}{TLC}}\mathllap{IC} = \mathrlap{IC_\text{working} + IC_\text{economic} + IC_\text{safety}}\hphantom{\underset{\displaystyle IC_\text{working} + IC_\text{economic} + IC_\text{safety}}{TC + IC + PC}} \tag{2}
$$

where

- $TC$ = transport cost (\$/yr)
- $IC$ = inventory cost (\$/yr)
- $PC$ = purchase cost (\$/yr)
- $IC_\text{working}$ = cost of working stock (\$/yr)
- $IC_\text{economic}$ = cost of economic stock (\$/yr)
- $IC_\text{safety}$ = cost of safety stock (\$/yr).

Of the terms of Eq. 1, it is the inventory cost that is taken up below, through the three terms of Eq. 2 in turn. In a deterministic world, total logistics cost (TLC) is minimized using average demand and transport lead times. For working and economic stock, the optimal level balances inventory cost ($IC$) with transport and purchase cost ($TC$ and $PC$), since an increase in the inventory cost of working and economic stock, $IC_{w+e}$, decreases $TC$ and $PC$. For safety stock, the optimal level is zero, and so is its inventory cost, $IC_s = 0$. In the stochastic, real world, TLC cannot simply be minimized. For working and economic stock, TLC can still be minimized using detrended averages; this is where the average still works. For safety stock, total profit (TP = TR – TLC) is maximized using actual (historical or synthetic) demand and transport lead times. If the inventory level is zero (out of stock) when a demand occurs, the result is a lost sale (zero revenue) or a backorder (likely at a lower price), and the optimal safety stock level balances the decrease in revenue from being out of stock with the increase in the inventory cost $IC_s$ due to holding or disposing of stock. Total logistics cost and its inventory cost split by role are those of Lecture 3.3 (Eq. 9 in Lecture 3.3 and Eq. 10 in Lecture 3.3).

These are the major decisions of the topic, and the rest of it plays out their implications. Everything in the course up to now has been in a deterministic world: location assumed a known, constant demand, and so did trucking, which was a big assumption, since the world has a lot of uncertainty. Working and economic stock can still be dealt with assuming a constant world. Uncertainty could be included, but there is a lot going on in a deterministic world already, and adding uncertainty would only make it more complicated. It is only safety stock that is at its core uncertain, and in a deterministic world there is no safety stock. For working and economic stock, the optimal level balances inventory cost with transport and production cost: a willingness to increase working and economic stock can be used to decrease the transport or the purchase cost, so one goes up as the other goes down, and the optimum is the best balance. In a deterministic world, the optimal level of safety stock is just zero. In the real world, which is stochastic, total logistics cost cannot simply be minimized. Working and economic stock can still be sized by minimizing total logistics cost with detrended averages, a situation in which averages still work, the question Lecture 1.1 raised of when it is appropriate to deal with averages. For safety stock, minimizing total cost does not always work, and the problem has to be framed instead as maximizing total profit, total revenue less total logistics cost. If the inventory level is zero when a demand occurs and the product cannot be produced instantaneously, one of two things happens. One is a lost sale: a customer who finds nothing on the shelf turns around and leaves, there is no way of making up for it, and the revenue is zero. The other is a backorder: the customer is willing to wait to receive the product when it is in stock again. The likely impact of allowing backorders is that the price has to be lower, everything else being equal, since most customers will wait only for a really good deal. A website offering a product at half the price of any other site, back in stock in two weeks, might find customers willing to wait two weeks to save 50%, each according to how much the wait matters to them; but to operate with low levels of safety stock, that website has to offer the product cheaper. There is no free lunch: the cost is paid in one place or the other, and the optimal safety stock level balances the decrease in revenue from being out of stock with the increase in the cost of holding or disposing of stock. That is easy for a product with very low obsolescence, which can simply be kept on the shelf all the time, but much product, such as groceries, spoils very quickly, and always having it on the shelf has a high inventory cost.

Lecture 1.1 explained why most logistics models minimize cost rather than maximize profit: when the quantity served is fixed and its price does not depend on how the system is configured, revenue is a constant. For safety stock the quantity sold depends on how much is held, so revenue is no longer a constant, and profit is what has to be maximized.

The inventory cost ($IC$) of working, economic, and safety stock can be calculated in the same general way, the way Lecture 3.3 calculated it for cycle stock (Eq. 11 in Lecture 3.3):

$$
\begin{aligned}
IC &= (\text{annual cost of holding one ton}) \\
&\quad \times (\text{average annual inventory level}) \\
&= vh\,(\$/\text{ton-yr}) \times q_I\,(\text{ton}) = (\$/\text{yr})
\end{aligned}
\tag{3}
$$

where

- $v$ = unit value of inventory (\$/ton)
- $h$ = inventory carrying rate, cost per \$ of inventory per year (1/yr)
- $q_I$ = average annual inventory level (ton).

The value for $v$ can be determined from the purchase price or production cost. The rate $h$ is usually not known directly, and is based on interest, warehousing, and obsolescence costs, as in Lecture 3.3 (Eq. 12 in Lecture 3.3). How $q_I$ in Eq. 3 is determined differs for working, economic, and safety stock.

Inventory cost is characterized the same way for all three types of stock, using the inventory carrying rate: how many dollars it costs per year to keep one dollar of inventory in stock. A 30% carrying rate means it costs \$30 per year to keep \$100 of inventory, \$300 per year to keep \$1,000, or \$3 per year to keep \$10. Its units are dollars per dollar per year, and cancelling the dollars is why its units are always written as one over a year; that is only a simplification, and it is better thought of as dollars per dollar-year of inventory, so the more expensive the inventory, the bigger the hit a 30% rate makes. The value $v$ has been taken so far as the purchase price, but the same formulation applies where the inventory is held at the point of production, with the production cost as its value: the truck shipments of Lecture 3.3 simply assumed someone at the origin producing the product. Where working, economic and safety stock mainly differ is in how the quantity held in inventory is determined, and most of the time the aim is to determine the optimal quantity, if at all possible.

## 2. Working stock

Working stock was ignored for truck transport in Lecture 3.3 since transit times were just a few days, compared to weeks between shipments. It is important for comparing international transport alternatives: ocean (weeks) against air cargo (hours).

Working stock was ignored for truck transport because the transit time was just a few days, compared to weeks between shipments, so to a first approximation only economic stock mattered, by far the bigger of the two. International transport may instead trade off ocean, which takes weeks, against air cargo, which takes hours for the same product, a really big difference in time, and the same product can switch from ocean to air cargo when the economics change. Flowers for Valentine’s Day, from a producer such as Colombia, fill dedicated cargo planes at that time of year, and textiles are compact enough that a great deal of their value fits on one cargo plane, as an alternative to ocean shipping.

Lecture 1.3’s view of a production system (Fig. 1 in Lecture 1.3) applies to transportation as well. Its input is raw material, held as raw material (RM) inventory, and once the product is produced it is held as finished goods inventory (FGI). The inventory held while the product is being produced, such as the two or three weeks a container spends on an ocean ship when transportation is the product being produced, is in transit: it is working stock, and from a production point of view it is work in process (WIP). The production system’s departure rate $r_d$ is the demand it satisfies, and the offered demand $r_f$ points into it, since a production system may not want to or be able to meet all of its demand: with a demand for 1,000 units by a deadline a week away, it might produce at most 800. Working stock is just another way of looking at work in process.

Lecture 1.3’s Little’s Law, repeated here as Eq. 4, relates the three averages:

$$
WIP = TH \times CT, \qquad TH = \frac{WIP}{CT}, \qquad CT = \frac{WIP}{TH},
\tag{4}
$$

where

- $TH$ = throughput
- $WIP$ = work-in-process
- $CT$ = cycle time.

Each is an average over a production system: throughput is its output per time period, in units per hour or any other rate; work-in-process is the number of units of product it holds; and cycle time is the time each unit spends in it.

So Little’s Law (Eq. 1 in Lecture 1.3) gives the average working stock as the throughput times the cycle time, and the average annual inventory level $q_I$ of Eq. 3 is found differently for working stock than for the cycle stock of Lecture 3.3:

$$
q_{I} = \begin{cases} \alpha q , & \text{cycle (economic) inventory} \\ n q t , & \text{in-transit (working) inventory} \end{cases}
\tag{5}
$$

where

- $\alpha$ = inter-shipment inventory fraction of Lecture 3.3 (dimensionless)
- $q$ = average shipment, order or production batch size (ton)
- $n$ = number of shipments per year (1/yr)
- $t$ = time each shipment spends in transit (yr).

For cycle stock the analysis is the same as for the truck shipments of Lecture 3.3: the average annual inventory level $q_I$ is the inventory fraction $\alpha$, which can be 0, 1/2 or 1, times the shipment size $q$ (Eq. 5). For in-transit, working stock, $q_I$ is the number of shipments times $q$ times $t$, and that is just Little’s Law: $nq$ is the throughput, $t$ is the cycle time, and $nqt$ is the WIP. Little’s Law and cycle inventory are two different results.

Little’s Law can only be used where the throughput, the work in process and the cycle time are not changing over time, the steady-state assumption of Lecture 1.3, and the first example depends on it:

Example 1: Inventory turns

Inventory turnover is a measure of the number of times inventory is sold. The value of inventory for a firm at the beginning of the year was \$10.2 million and \$12.4 million at the end of the year, and its annual cost of goods sold (COGS) was \$226 million. Determine its inventory turnover during the year.

Inventory turnover is how the performance of a company is evaluated: one company might turn its inventory over five times a year and another in the same industry eight or nine times, and the second is a lot more profitable because it is not carrying as much inventory. Inventory turnover, the number of turns per year, is one over the cycle time, just as, for the truck shipments of Lecture 3.3, the number of shipments per year $n$ is one over the shipment interval, and by Little’s Law (Eq. 4) it is the throughput over the WIP:

$$
\mathit{turns} = \frac{1}{CT} = \frac{TH}{WIP}
\tag{6}
$$

In Eq. 6, the WIP is the average of the beginning and ending inventory, and the throughput is the annual cost of goods sold. The catch is that two values of inventory are given, not one, and Little’s Law needs stationary data, while here inventory increased over the year. Whether that is an increasing trend that would invalidate Little’s Law cannot be answered from the data given. Using the average assumes the difference is just random variation, and that cannot simply be assumed: it has to be verified, for example by looking at previous years to see whether inventory bounces around at roughly the same level. If it does, the data can be averaged. Little’s Law, like a chatbot’s result, is never used blindly, and although formal measures of stationarity are not taken up here, stationary data is usually obvious just from looking at it.

By Little’s Law, the turnover is

$$
CT = \frac{WIP}{TH} = \frac{\left( \frac{10.2 + 12.4}{2} \right)}{226} = \frac{11.3}{226} = \frac{1}{20} \Rightarrow 20 \text{ turns per year}

$$

The Assumptions check of Lecture 1.2 asks why it is necessary to verify that the difference in beginning and ending inventory is due to random variation and not due to a long-term increase in inventory. The answer is that Little’s Law only works if WIP is not changing, and taking the average is only a good estimate if the inventory is in steady state.

Code block 1 does the same calculation in Julia:

```julia
# Code block 1: inventory turns by Little's Law
@show WIP = (10.2 + 12.4)/2   # average inventory ($ million)
TH = 226                      # annual cost of goods sold ($ million/yr)
@show CT = WIP/TH             # cycle time (yr)
@show turns = 1/CT            # turns per year
```

```text
WIP = (10.2 + 12.4) / 2 = 11.3
CT = WIP / TH = 0.05
turns = 1 / CT = 20.0
```

```text
20.0
```

20 turns per year

Example 2: In-transit inventory and suppliers

Determine the annual cost of the raw material in transit from a supplier in Shanghai, and whether a domestic supplier should replace it.

Example 2(a): In-transit inventory cost

Currently, a factory in Los Angeles imports 12 containers per year from a supplier in Shanghai, each CL (container load) has 15 tons of raw material. Each ton of RM costs \$7,000 and loses 10% of its value after three months. Each container spends 21 days in transit, and its transport cost is \$2,620. Determine the annual in-transit inventory cost for RM.

Little’s Law can be put to work in supply chain analysis, and in-transit inventory is a good example. The terminology is the same as for the truck shipments of Lecture 3.3, from a slightly different angle, starting with the shipment size and the shipment frequency:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Shipment size: } q &= 15 \text{ ton/CL} \\ \text{Shipment frequency: } n &= 12 \text{ CL/yr}\end{aligned}

$$

The cycle time is the 21 days spent in transit, divided by 365.25 to put it in years:

$$
CT : t = \frac{21}{365.25} \text{ yr}

$$

The throughput, in tons per year, is the 12 containers times 15 tons per container:

$$
TH : n q = 12 ( 15 ) = 180 \text{ ton/yr}

$$

Little’s Law then gives the WIP as the throughput times the cycle time, $nqt$. That is the average working stock level $q_I$, a quantity and not yet a cost:

$$
WIP = TH \cdot CT : q_{I} = n q t = 12 ( 15 ) \frac{21}{365.25} = 10.35 \text{ ton}

$$

Each container spends only 21 days in transit and there are 12 of them, so a container is in transit only about 69% of the year, unlike the truck shipments of Lecture 3.3, which followed one after another and so were in transit all of the time:

$$
\frac{12 ( 21 )}{365.25} = 69\% \text{ yr}

$$

Its cost needs the carrying rate. The raw material loses 10% of its value after three months, a quarter of a year, so by the percent-reduction interval of Eq. 13 in Lecture 3.3 its obsolescence rate works out to

$$
h_{\text{obs}} = \frac{x_{h}}{t_{h}} = \frac{0.1}{0.25} = 0.4

$$

Adding to it the 5% interest and 6% warehousing of Eq. 12 in Lecture 3.3 gives the carrying rate, per year:

$$
h = 0.05 + 0.06 + h_{\text{obs}} = 0.51 ( 1 / \text{yr} )

$$

The in-transit inventory cost then follows from Eq. 3, and it is that cost that is useful for supplier selection:

$$
I C_{w} = v h q_{I} = 7000 ( 0.51 ) 10.35 = \$36{,}946.20 \text{ /yr}

$$

The units carried through to the cost, $[ \$ / \text{ton } ( 1 / \text{yr} ) \text{ ton} = \$ / \text{yr} ]$, are the Units check of Lecture 1.2. Code block 2 does the same calculation in Julia:

```julia
# Code block 2: annual in-transit inventory cost, international supplier
q = 15                        # ton/CL, shipment size
n = 12                        # CL/yr, shipment frequency
@show t = 21/365.25           # yr, transit time (CT)
@show TH = n*q                # ton/yr, annual throughput
@show qI = n*q*t              # ton, average inventory in transit (WIP)
@show n*t                     # share of a year a container is in transit
xh = 0.1                      # value lost over the period
th = 0.25                     # yr, period of value loss
@show hobs = xh/th            # 1/yr, obsolescence rate
hint = 0.05                   # 1/yr, interest
hwh = 0.06                    # 1/yr, warehousing
@show h = hint + hwh + hobs   # 1/yr, total annual carrying rate
v = 7000                      # $/ton, value per ton
@show ICw = v*h*qI            # $/yr, annual in-transit inventory cost
```

```text
t = 21 / 365.25 = 0.057494866529774126
TH = n * q = 180
qI = n * q * t = 10.349075975359343
n * t = 0.6899383983572895
hobs = xh / th = 0.4
h = hint + hwh + hobs = 0.51
ICw = v * h * qI = 36946.20123203285
```

```text
36946.20123203285
```

\$36,946 per year

Example 2(b): Supplier selection

Continuing Ex. 2(a), a domestic supplier has been identified with a cost of \$9,000 per ton. 12 truckloads (TLs) per year, each containing 15 tons of RM, would be shipped 200 miles in one day. TL revenue per loaded mile is \$2. Determine whether the domestic supplier should be used.

The question is whether the premium the domestic supplier charges per ton is worth paying to switch from the international supplier. The analysis is the same as for Ex. 2(a), with trucks in place of containers, but the decision cannot be made on the working inventory cost alone, because that does not capture everything: the alternatives have to be compared on total logistics cost. For the international supplier, that is the number of shipments times the cost per shipment, plus the working inventory cost already calculated, plus the product cost, the price per ton times the tons shipped each year:

$$
\begin{aligned}\text{Int: } TLC_{1} &= TC + I C_{w} + PC \\ &= n c_{CL} + v h q_{I} + n v q \\ &= 12 ( 2620 ) + 7000 ( 0.51 ) 10.35 + 12 ( 7000 ) 15 \\ &= 31{,}440 + 36{,}946 + 1{,}260{,}000 = \$1{,}328{,}386 \text{ /yr}\end{aligned}

$$

For the domestic supplier, the truckload cost is the \$2 per mile times the 200 miles, \$400 per truckload:

$$
\text{Dom: } r_{TL} = \$2 \text{ /mi, } d = 200 \text{ mi} , c_{TL} = r_{TL} d = \$400

$$

Its average inventory level, with each truckload one day in transit, is much smaller, under half a ton against more than ten:

$$
q_{I} = n q t = 12 ( 15 ) \frac{1}{365.25} = 0.4928 \text{ ton}

$$

Each of the 12 truckloads is in transit for one day, so a truckload is in transit only about 3.3% of the year, against the container’s 69%:

$$
\frac{12 ( 1 )}{365.25} = 3.3\% \text{ yr}

$$

Doing the same calculation for it gives a higher total logistics cost than the international supplier’s:

$$
\begin{aligned}TLC_{2} &= TC + I C_{w} + PC \\ &= n c_{TL} + v h q_{I} + n v q \\ &= 12 ( 400 ) + 9000 ( 0.51 ) 0.4928 + 12 ( 9000 ) 15 \\ &= 4{,}800 + 2{,}262 + 1{,}620{,}000 = \$1{,}627{,}062 \text{ /yr}\end{aligned}

$$

In each total, the three parts add back to it, the Balance check of Lecture 1.2. So the international supplier is selected, and the domestic supplier would have to lower its price to compete. All of this is easily done in a short Julia script: a quote for the ocean shipment is all that is needed, with no mapping or optimization.

Code block 3 is that script, for both suppliers:

```julia
# Code block 3: total logistics cost of each supplier
# international, from Shanghai: n, q, h, v and ICw as in Code block 2
cCL = 2620                    # $/CL, transport cost per container
TC1 = n*cCL                   # $/yr, transport cost
PC1 = n*v*q                   # $/yr, purchase cost
TLC1 = TC1 + ICw + PC1        # $/yr, total logistics cost
# domestic, by truckload
rTL = 2                       # $/mi, TL revenue per loaded mile
dTL = 200                     # mi, distance
@show cTL = rTL*dTL           # $/TL, truckload charge
t2 = 1/365.25                 # yr, transit time
@show qI2 = n*q*t2            # ton, average inventory in transit
@show n*t2                    # share of the year a truck is in transit
v2 = 9000                     # $/ton, value per ton
ICw2 = v2*h*qI2               # $/yr, in-transit inventory cost
TC2 = n*cTL                   # $/yr, transport cost
PC2 = n*v2*q                  # $/yr, purchase cost
TLC2 = TC2 + ICw2 + PC2       # $/yr, total logistics cost
# the two suppliers' costs, side by side
prt(DataFrame(supplier = ["international", "domestic"], TC = [TC1, TC2],
              ICw = round.([ICw, ICw2], digits = 2), PC = [PC1, PC2],
              TLC = round.([TLC1, TLC2], digits = 2)))
```

```text
cTL = rTL * dTL = 400
qI2 = n * q * t2 = 0.4928131416837782
n * t2 = 0.03285420944558522
       supplier      TC        ICw         PC           TLC
───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  international  31,440  36,946.20  1,260,000  1,328,386.20
       domestic   4,800   2,262.01  1,620,000  1,627,062.01
```

The international supplier’s total logistics cost, \$1,328,386 per year, is below the domestic supplier’s \$1,627,062: keep the supplier in Shanghai

The same reading of Little’s Law gives the time a ton spends at a distribution center, and the time a ton spends in a production plan, two quantities the lectures that computed their inventories did not report:

Example 3: Dwell at a DC and through a plan

Determine, by Little’s Law, the average time a ton spends at a distribution center and in a production plan, from the inventories two earlier lectures computed.

Example 3(a): Dwell at the Memphis DC

In Ex. 2(b) in Lecture 3.4, with no coordination at the distribution center (DC) in Memphis, the DC holds on average half of each of its three inbound shipments, 6.647, 2.0625 and 8.25 tons, and 875 tons pass through it each year. Determine the average time a ton spends at the DC.

By Little’s Law, the DC’s average inventory is its WIP and the tons passing through it each year are its throughput:

$$
\begin{aligned}
CT = \frac{WIP}{TH} &= \frac{6.647 + 2.0625 + 8.25}{875} \\
&= \frac{16.96}{875} \\
&= 0.01938 \text{ yr} \times 365.25 = 7.08 \text{ days}
\end{aligned}

$$

Code block 4 does the same calculation in Julia:

```julia
THdc = 875                            # ton/yr, throughput of the DC
@show CTyr = WIPdc/THdc               # yr, mean dwell
@show CTdc = CTyr*365.25              # days, mean dwell
```

```text
CTyr = WIPdc / THdc = 0.019382285714285713
```

Example 3(b): Cycle time of a production plan

The plan of Ex. 1 in Lecture 4.3 delivers 20, 10 and 15 tons in its three months, and carries 25 tons of inventory at stage 2 between months 1 and 2 and 15 tons between months 2 and 3. Determine the average time a ton spends in the plan, from stage 1 to delivery.

The inventory carried between periods, in ton-months, is the plan’s WIP, and the tons it delivers over the three months are its throughput:

$$
CT = \frac{WIP}{TH} = \frac{25 + 15}{20 + 10 + 15} = \frac{40}{45} = 0.889 \text{ month}

$$

## 3. Economic stock

Economic stock is held to allow cheaper production or transport, and is of two kinds, cycle and anticipation stock. Cycle (economic) inventory is held to allow cheaper large shipments, orders or production batches: the per-unit cost falls with size, but the holding cost rises, so the best trade-off is found. Anticipation (economic) inventory is product that is cheaper to purchase or produce early, as when a product is on sale, discounted, or discontinued, or with production that occurs throughout the year ahead of a single peak selling period (e.g., Christmas decorations).

The key trade-off for cycle stock is that the cost per unit falls with size, as the figures for truck shipments in Lecture 3.3 showed (Fig. 4 in Lecture 3.3): the more that is shipped, the cheaper the cost per unit, but the holding cost rises, and the whole game is to find the best trade-off, which is what determining the optimal truckload size did. Anticipation stock is product that is cheaper to produce or purchase early, as when a product is on sale, discounted or discontinued and is stocked up on. With a peak season such as Christmas, it might be a lot cheaper to produce throughout the year and accumulate enough stock for the season than to wait until two months before Christmas and produce at a breakneck pace. Anticipation stock is not analyzed here; the focus is on cycle stock. The inventory in the production-inventory networks of Lectures 4.3 and 4.4 is economic stock. It is held so that production capacity can be more efficiently utilized, for example, to save on setup or switchover costs, or to produce ahead of a stage that does not have the capacity to satisfy a period’s demand.

Cycle stock is what the optimal truckload shipment size of Lecture 3.3 traded against transport cost (Eq. 18 in Lecture 3.3 and Eq. 19 in Lecture 3.3), with no purchase cost, since within the United States the purchase cost was assumed to be the same. Purchase cost matters mostly when international is compared with domestic: purchasing overseas can make the purchase cost a lot less, and the trade-off is paying more for the logistics of getting the product to the United States, as in Ex. 2. For a truckload there was a simple analytical formula for the optimal size, but not for less than truckload, whose minimum had to be found numerically. More generally, this is the notion of the economic order quantity, or EOQ.

Lecture 3.3’s truckload model is repeated here, as Eq. 7 and Eq. 8, since the EOQ is set against it. The total annual logistics cost for TL shipments is given by the sum of the transportation cost (TC) and the cycle inventory costs (IC) at the origin and destination, specifically:

$$
TLC_{TL}(q) = \frac{f}{q}\max\bigl\{ c_{TL}, MC_{TL} \bigr\} + \alpha v h q
\approx \frac{f}{q}\, r d + \alpha v h q.
\tag{7}
$$

Minimizing with respect to $q$ yields

$$
q_{TL}^{*} = \min\left\{ \sqrt{\frac{f \max\{ r d, MC_{TL} \}}{\alpha v h}},\;
q_{\max} \right\} \approx \sqrt{\frac{f r d}{\alpha v h}},
\tag{8}
$$

where the approximation ignores the minimum charge and maximum payload restrictions.

- $TLC_{TL}(q)$ = total logistics cost of TL shipments of size $q$ (\$/yr)
- $c_{TL}$ = TL transport charge (\$)
- $MC_{TL}$ = TL minimum charge (\$)
- $q_{TL}^{*}$ = optimal TL shipment size (ton).

and, as in Lecture 3.3,

- $f$ = annual demand (ton/yr)
- $r$ = TL revenue per loaded mile (\$/mi)
- $d$ = distance (mi)
- $q_{\max}$ = maximum payload of a truck (ton).

The economic order quantity model finds the optimal quantity (termed the EOQ) that minimizes the cost of the number of shipments, orders or production batches and the cost of holding them as inventory. It comes from an early (1913) paper, “How Many Parts to Make at Once,” in Factory, The Magazine of Management, by Ford W. Harris, that introduced a simple square-root formula to determine how many parts to make. In Harris’s own words, an increase in the size of the order results in an increased interest charge and a decreased set-up cost, and the curves of the two show a minimum total cost.1

Harris’s paper, more than 110 years old, could be called the start of what became scientific management and industrial engineering, before the field even had that name. It was the first time people took note that the problems of a factory could be looked at mathematically, and the realization that an optimum could actually be found, which was not on the radar for most people, spread through factories across the United States and had a big impact on the field. Harris’s own chart (Fig. 1) shows the classic inventory cost increasing with the quantity, as the transport cost did for truck shipments, while in manufacturing a setup can be spread over more units, so its cost per unit decreases; added together, they give a U-shaped curve whose minimum point is the optimum. The equation is the same as the truckload model’s, except that $\alpha$ is fixed at one half, since there is no transportation to give other options, and the result is the classic square-root formula for $q^*$, two times $f$ times the fixed cost over $vh$. For truck shipments the fixed cost was the transport cost spread over more units, but in general it can be a setup cost, to set up to produce a batch of product, or the cost of placing an order, when the question is the optimal order size. The fixed cost takes different guises in these situations, and they all result in essentially the same formula.

Figure 1: Harris’s cost curves for a small connector: the set-up cost per piece falls and the interest and depreciation on stock rise with the manufacturing quantity, and their sum is lowest at the EOQ, Harris’s economical lot size.2

The EOQ problem is stated as Model 1, a special case of the minimum-TLC shipment size model of Lecture 3.3 (Model 1 in Lecture 3.3): each of its differences is a choice of that model’s data, a fixed cost per batch in place of the truckload charge, $\alpha$ set at one half, a payload too large to bind, and a less-than-truckload (LTL) charge too high for LTL ever to be selected.

minimize: total logistics cost of producing, ordering ortransporting a product ~~point-to-point (P2P)~~periodically, ~~transport~~ fixed cost plus cycle inventory

solve for:
(a) average batch, order orshipment size, a positive weight in tons or number of units~~;~~.
~~(b) service that carries it, TL or LTL.~~

subject to:
~~(a) payload: a TL shipment is no larger than one full truckload;~~
~~(b) validity: an LTL shipment stays within the range the LTL rate estimate was fitted on.~~ none

assumptions:
(a) annual demand is known and constant;
(b) product value, carrying rate and inventory fraction do not depend on shipment size;
(c) in-transit inventory is the same for ~~TL and LTL~~ every size, so it is not a relevant cost~~.~~;
(d) each batch, order or shipment arrives all at once, so the inventory fraction is one half.

Model 1: Economic order quantity

Special case of Model 1: Minimum-TLC shipment size in Lecture 3.3

Model 1 formulation: Economic order quantity

The total annual logistics cost of batches of size $q$ is that of the truckload model, Eq. 7, with a fixed cost $c_o$ per batch in place of the truckload charge and $\alpha = \tfrac{1}{2}$:

$$
\min_{q > 0} \; TLC(q) = \frac{f}{q}\, c_o + \frac{1}{2}\, v h q
\tag{9}
$$

and setting its derivative with respect to $q$ to zero gives the economic order quantity:

$$
q^{*} = \sqrt{\frac{2 f c_o}{v h}}
\tag{10}
$$

where

- $q$ = batch or order size (units)
- $c_o$ = fixed cost per batch, of production, setup, transport or ordering (\$)
- $q^{*}$ = economic order quantity (units).

No Logjam function computes the EOQ, so its implementation is written out here:

Model 1 implementation: Economic order quantity

```julia
# Model: economic order quantity
eoq(f, co, v, h) = sqrt(2*f*co/(v*h))
```

```text
eoq (generic function with 1 method)
```

Example 4: EOQ for setup costs

A manufacturer produces a replacement part with steady annual demand of 100,000 units. Each production run requires a \$250 setup for cleaning, tooling, and inspection. Finished parts are worth \$100 each, and holding inventory incurs costs of about 30% of their value per year for capital, storage, and obsolescence. Production is assumed instantaneous, and demand is constant. Determine the optimal number of parts to produce per run to minimize the combined annual cost of setups and inventory.

With steady demand and a setup cost given, the data can be plugged into the formula to solve for $q^*$, just as for the periodic truckload problem of Lecture 3.3. What was done there for the optimal truckload size is done here more generally, and this is the classic type of EOQ.

Example 4(a): EOQ by hand

Determine the number of parts to produce per run by hand, from Eq. 9 and Eq. 10.

With $f = 100{,}000$ units per year, $c_o = \$250$ per run, $v = \$100$ per part and $h = 0.3$ per year, the total logistics cost of Eq. 9 is a function of the run size $q$ alone:

$$
TLC(q) = \frac{f}{q}\, c_o + \frac{1}{2}\, v h q
= \frac{100{,}000}{q}\, 250 + \frac{1}{2}\, 100 (0.3)\, q

$$

Its minimum is at the EOQ of Eq. 10, with the same four values:

$$
q^{*} = \sqrt{\frac{2 f c_o}{v h}}
= \sqrt{\frac{2 (100{,}000)\, 250}{100 (0.3)}}
\approx 1{,}291 \text{ parts/run}

$$

The Assumptions check of Lecture 1.2 is on the one half in Eq. 9, which holds because production is instantaneous and demand is constant, as the statement assumes. Harris put the condition this way: the average stock is one-half of the lot size if the movement is regular, and if the movement is irregular, as it generally is, an additional complication is introduced.3

$q^{*} =$ 1,291 parts per run

Example 4(b): EOQ in code and by brute force

Determine the number of parts per run with the implementation of Model 1 and by a brute-force search of Eq. 9 over every whole number of parts, and compare both with Ex. 4(a).

```julia
v = 100                 # $/part, value of a finished part
h = 0.3                 # 1/yr, carrying rate
qᵒ = eoq(f, co, v, h)   # parts/run
```

```julia
TLCbf, qbf = minimum((totlogcost(q, co, f, 1/2, v, h), q)
                     for q ∈ 1:f)

```

Each run size is paired with its cost, and minimum compares the pairs by cost first, so it returns the least cost together with its run size, as Code block 4 of Lecture 5.2 does for routes.

## 4. One-time safety stock

### One-time versus periodic safety stock

Safety stock is held to buffer the effects of uncertainty, and it comes in two kinds. One-time safety stock is the case of uncertain demand and of not being able to carry inventory: unmet demand is a lost sale, excess (expired or obsolete) product is disposed of, and the optimal policy is a trade-off between lost profit and disposal cost. Periodic safety stock is the case of uncertain demand and/or transport lead time and of being able to carry inventory: unmet demand is either a lost sale or a backorder, excess product is carried over to the next period, and the optimal policy is a trade-off with lost profit or backorder cost and inventory carrying cost. Periodic safety stock is the subject of Lecture 6.2.

One-time and periodic safety stock are distinguished just as one-time and periodic truck shipments were, and the periodic case is a little more complicated. Both deal with uncertain demand: if demand were certain, safety stock would never be needed. The important thing for one-time safety stock is that inventory cannot be carried. With daily production, for example, whatever product is left at the end of the day is obsolete, essentially worthless, and cannot be carried over to the next day. This is the classic news vendor problem, named for the idea that nobody wants a day-old newspaper; it is called one-time safety stock here because, although it is essentially the same problem, it is solved differently from the technique most textbooks use. Any unmet demand is a lost sale, so whatever revenue a customer who is not served would have brought is lost, while with periodic safety stock unmet demand can also be backordered, the customer willing to wait a day or two for a product that does not expire in one period. The optimal policy is then the trade-off between lost profit and disposal cost. The disposal cost need not be just what was spent to make the product: a product that cost \$5 to make and sells for \$10 might be salvaged for \$5 at a retailer of odd merchandise, while a hazardous product might cost something to dispose of, so the disposal cost can be positive or negative relative to that.

### Operating profit

If the demand $d$ for tomorrow is known, then $q = d$ units should be produced, and the only interesting question is how cheaply the units can be produced. If the demand $D$ for tomorrow is unknown, then how many units $q$ to produce becomes an interesting question. Batch production and consumption can be assumed $\Rightarrow IC_{w+e} = 0$, and the operating profit if $q$ units are produced and demand turns out to be $d_i$ is:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\text{Profit: } & \pi(q, d_{i}) = \begin{cases} p d_{i} - c q , & \text{if } q > d_{i} \\ p q - c q = (p - c) q , & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \\
& \hphantom{\pi(q, d_{i})} = \boxed{p \min\{q, d_{i}\} - c q} \\[8pt]
\text{Lost sales: } & \max\{d_{i} - q, 0\} \\[8pt]
\text{Lost profit: } & (p - c) \max\{d_{i} - q, 0\}
\end{aligned}
\tag{11}
$$

where

- $\pi(q, d_i)$ = operating profit on a day of demand $d_i$ when $q$ units are produced (\$)
- $q$ = units produced, before the day’s demand is known
- $d_i$ = demand on day $i$ (units)
- $p$ = unit price (\$/unit)
- $c$ = unit cost (\$/unit).

Operating profit includes both the cost and the revenue side. If tomorrow’s demand were known, $q$ would simply be set equal to it, and the only question would be how cheaply the units can be produced, a matter of minimizing cost. The capital $D$ indicates that demand is stochastic: it is not known, and how many to produce becomes the interesting question. With batch production and consumption, all of the working and economic inventory goes to zero, so the only reason not to produce the known demand is that the demand is not known.

For any quantity $q$ produced and demand $d_i$ realized, there are two possibilities. If more was produced than the demand, revenue is earned only on the actual demand: with five units sold and ten produced, the revenue is five times the price, but the cost is $c$ times ten units, and the profit that day can very likely be negative. If demand equals or exceeds the quantity produced, the price is received on everything produced: with a demand of 15 and ten produced, five customers are lost sales, and the revenue is for the ten produced, less the cost of producing them. Since $q$ appears in both terms, it can be taken out, leaving $p - c$, the operating unit profit, the price received less the cost; if the price equaled the cost the profit would be zero, so to be interesting the price has to exceed the cost. The two conditions can be replaced, without an if statement, by the smaller of the quantity produced and the actual demand, times the price, less the cost times the quantity produced: this is the basic news vendor profit equation. Lost sales are positive when demand is greater than the quantity and zero when too much is produced, though then there is product to dispose of, and lost profit is the unit profit times the larger of that difference and zero.

One-time safety stock is a data-rich problem, and the data should be leveraged as much as possible, which is why the standard news vendor approach is not used here. That approach assumes a distribution for demand, such as a Poisson, normal, negative binomial or gamma distribution, which raises the question of how to know which distribution; fitting one to a lot of data and then using only the distribution is like having a room full of great data and throwing it all away for a mathematical substitute. The textbook approach looks for the critical fractile of the cumulative distribution, and there may be some reason to do that, but none has been seen for this problem. The approach taken here, which uses the data directly, is not found in textbooks, so an AI tool would likely say that it cannot be done this way.

### Equal costs under and over

When a unit under and a unit over cost the same, the problem is the minisum in one dimension of Lecture 2.1 (Model 8 in Lecture 2.1). Each data point is an existing facility (EF) of weight one, and the solution is their median (Eq. 5 in Lecture 2.1), found by the same procedure. Ex. 5 shows it, with a cost in time rather than profit:

Example 5: Pre-fill level of a test tank

A testing center has a device that is able to use ultrasonic waves transmitted within a special solution to detect defects in parts like aircraft engines. The part is placed in a tank that, in order to operate correctly, is filled with just enough solution to submerge the part; the solution is then drained from the tank and disposed of since it can become contaminated during testing. Currently, test results are being delayed because it is time-consuming to fill the tank with the solution. In order to speed up testing, a suggestion has been made to consider pre-filling the tank and then either adding or draining the solution as needed to submerge a part. The following demand data is available regarding the cubic volume of solution that was needed to test recent parts:

$$
237, 214, 161, 146, 331, 159, 423, 332, 139, 327, 152, 98, 116
$$

Determine the cubic volume of solution that should be pre-filled in the tank to minimize the time required to submerge the part, given that the tank can be filled or drained at the same rate.

It is a good idea to look at the data to see if there is a pattern to the data and check to see if there are any anomalous, outlier data that could be erroneous. If anything is found, it might be possible to ask whoever provided the data about the issue before doing any further analysis. If some data is in error, then it can be deleted; outlier data should not automatically be eliminated unless it is a real error.

It is easy to display 1-D, a little harder but doable for 2-D, and difficult for 3+ degree data, where the best that can usually be done is to look at different 1- and 2-D cross-sections of the data. For this data, since there is no time element, a histogram is used instead of a scatter or line plot (Fig. 2).


Determine the pre-fill level by hand, as the median of the demands.

Each part is an EF of weight one, so $W = 13$, and with $d_{(j)}$ the $j$th smallest demand, in order the demands and their running count are

$$
\def\tight#1{\kern-3pt #1\kern-3pt}
\begin{array}{l|ccccccccccccc}
d_{(j)} & \tight{98} & \tight{116} & \tight{139} & \tight{146} & \tight{152} & \tight{159} & \tight{\mathbf{161}} & \tight{214} & \tight{237} & \tight{327} & \tight{331} & \tight{332} & \tight{423} \\
j & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 & \mathbf{7} & 8 & 9 & 10 & 11 & 12 & 13

$$

The first $j$ at which the count reaches $W/2 = 6.5$, as in Eq. 5 in Lecture 2.1, is $j = 7$, so the pre-fill level is the seventh demand in order, 161.

Example 5(b): Pre-fill level in code

Determine the pre-fill level in code by the median procedure of Lecture 2.1, and the level that minimizes the total time numerically, and compare both with Ex. 5(a).

Not seeing anything unusual in the histogram, the next step can be to develop a model that captures the “cost” of different pre-fill levels, where the cost, in this case, can be the time required to either fill or drain the tank from the pre-fill level, where it is assumed that, for a given volume of solution, the fill and drain times are the same since their rates are the same, and the time to fill or drain the tank from the pre-fill level for each part is

$$
\text{Time: } t(q, d_i) = \bigl| d_i - q \bigr|
\tag{12}
$$

where

- $t(q, d_i)$ = time to fill or drain the tank from the pre-fill level for part $i$
- $q$ = pre-fill level (cubic volume)
- $d_i$ = volume of solution needed to test part $i$ (cubic volume).

A unit under and a unit over take the same time, so the median procedure of Lecture 2.1 applies unchanged, in the code Lecture 2.2 gave it (Ex. 1(b) in Lecture 2.2): sort the demands, give each part a weight of one, and stop at the first part whose running total of weight reaches half the total. Code block 9 runs it first, then minimizes the total time of Eq. 12 over the 13 parts by brute force and numerically, and Fig. 3 draws the total time against the pre-fill level, with the minimum the search finds in maroon:

```julia
# Code block 9: pre-fill level by the median procedure, then numerically
# the median procedure of Lecture 2.1, as Lecture 2.2 coded it
ds = sort(d)                                # demands in order
w = ones(Int, length(ds))                   # each part an EF, weight one
@show W = sum(w)
@show j = findfirst(>=(W / 2), cumsum(w))   # first running total >= W/2
@show qmed = ds[j]

# the total time over the 13 parts, minimized
using Optim
ft(q, di) = abs(di - q)                  # time for a single part
fTT(q, d) = sum(ft(q, di) for di in d)   # total time
# brute force first: each whole-number level, one at a time
TTmin, qmin = minimum((fTT(q, d), q) for q ∈ 0:maximum(d))
@show qmin
qᵒ = optimize(q -> fTT(q, d), 0, maximum(d)).minimizer
@show round(qᵒ, digits = 2)
@show round(fTT(qᵒ, d), digits = 2);
```

```text
W = sum(w) = 13
j = findfirst((>=)(W / 2), cumsum(w)) = 7
qmed = ds[j] = 161
qmin = 161
round(qᵒ, digits = 2) = 161.0
round(fTT(qᵒ, d), digits = 2) = 1054.0
```

Show the code that draws this figure

```julia

ax = Axis(fig[1, 1]; xlabel = "Pre-fill level", ylabel = "Total time",
          xlabelsize = 15, ylabelsize = 15,
          xticklabelsize = 13, yticklabelsize = 13)
optc = colorant"#b23a48"                 # an optimum, as in Lecture 2.2
lines!(ax, 0:maximum(d), q -> fTT(q, d); color = bluec, linewidth = 2)
scatter!(ax, [qᵒ], [fTT(qᵒ, d)]; color = optc, markersize = 13)
fig
```

The Landmark check of Lecture 1.2 is that the numerical minimum, at 161, is the median found by hand in Ex. 5(a) and by the procedure in Code block 9, an answer known before the search was run.

$q^{*} =$ 161, at a total time of 1054

Example 5(c): Extreme outlier

Determine the pre-fill level if the demand of 423 had instead been 1,423.

Since the solution is only as good as the model and data used to generate it, it is helpful to try to determine how robust the solution is with respect to the data that was used and the assumptions behind the model. Starting with data robustness, one thing that can be checked is what if there had been an extreme outlier in the data. For example, if the 423 demand was instead 1,423, would the solution change significantly?

```julia
# Code block 11: the pre-fill level with an extreme outlier
d2 = copy(d)             # a copy: d2 = d would only point to d, and
d2[d2 .== 423] .= 1423   # a change to d2 would also change d
qᵒ2 = optimize(q -> fTT(q, d2), 0, maximum(d2)).minimizer
@show round(qᵒ2, digits = 2)
@show round(fTT(qᵒ2, d2), digits = 2);
```

```text
round(qᵒ2, digits = 2) = 161.0
round(fTT(qᵒ2, d2), digits = 2) = 2054.0
```

Although, as expected, the total time increases by 1,000, it might seem surprising that the optimal pre-fill level remains unchanged. The reason for this is, for this particular objective function, the optimal solution is the value of the median demand point. Any unit increase in the solution would increase by one unit the times of all of the demands less and decrease by one unit the times of all demands greater than the solution. Since the unit cost of filling and draining are the same and, being the median point, there are equal numbers of points less than and greater than the solution, the optimal solution remains unchanged. This is Lecture 2.1’s argument for the median location, and its result as well: moving Asheville, the westernmost of the cities on I-40, all the way to California leaves the minisum location where it was, since the median procedure uses only the order of the facilities, never their coordinates (Fig. 7 in Lecture 2.1). Raising the largest demand from 423 to 1,423 is the same move, the last point on the line taken farther out with the order unchanged.

### Unequal costs under and over

When a unit under and a unit over cost different amounts, as filling and draining do in Ex. 5(d), which follows, and as a lost sale and a disposed unit do, the quantity is the one that minimizes the total overage and underage cost over the demand history, stated as Model 2, a generalization of the minisum in one dimension of Lecture 2.1 (Model 8 in Lecture 2.1), and formulated as Eq. 13. That minisum, with each EF of weight one, is its special case: with $c_{\text{over}} = c_{\text{under}}$, a unit under and a unit over cost the same, and minimizing the total cost is minimizing the total of $\lvert d_i - q \rvert$, as in Ex. 5(a) to (c), the demands the EFs and the quantity the location of the new facility. Ex. 5(d) is the case $c_{\text{over}} = 1$ and $c_{\text{under}} = 2$, a unit drained taking half the time of a unit filled.

minimize: total ~~weighted distance from a new facility (NF) to the $m$ existing facilities (EFs) along a line~~ overage and underage cost over the demand history, when the same quantity is set for each demand before that demand is known

solve for:
(a) ~~location $x$ of the NF, any point along the line~~ quantity set for each demand, the same for every demand.

subject to: none

assumptions:
(a) ~~facilities lie on a single line, so distance is one-dimensional; a two-dimensional problem with rectilinear distance is solved by applying the model once along each axis~~ demand is stationary, so the history represents the variability of any one demand;
(b) ~~each EF’s weight $w_i$ is known, and the EFs can be placed in order along the line, but their actual coordinates are not needed~~ overage cost of a unit over and underage cost of a unit under are constant;
(c) inventory cannot be carried from one demand to the next.

Model 2: One-time safety stock

Generalization of Model 8: Minisum in one dimension in Lecture 2.1

Model 2 formulation: One-time safety stock

With an overage cost $c_{\text{over}}$ for each unit the quantity exceeds a demand and an underage cost $c_{\text{under}}$ for each unit a demand exceeds the quantity, the quantity solves

$$
\min_{q \ge 0} \; C(q) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} \Bigl[\, c_{\text{over}} \max\{q - d_i, 0\} + c_{\text{under}} \max\{d_i - q, 0\} \,\Bigr]
\tag{13}
$$

where

- $C(q)$ = total overage and underage cost over the history
- $c_{\text{over}}$ = overage cost, of each unit the quantity exceeds a demand (\$/unit)
- $c_{\text{under}}$ = underage cost, of each unit a demand exceeds the quantity (\$/unit)
- $N$ = number of demands in the history.

No Logjam function computes it, so its implementation is written out here:

Model 2 implementation: One-time safety stock

```julia
# Model: one-time safety stock
# One demand's cost (c_over, c_under given), total, and best quantity
fc(q, di) = c_over*max(q - di, 0) + c_under*max(di - q, 0)
fC(q, d) = sum(fc(q, di) for di in d)
mincost(d) = minimum((fC(q, d), q) for q ∈ 0:maximum(d))

```

- 1 Each whole number from 0 to the largest demand is tried in turn, and the one with the least total cost is kept. No quantity above the largest demand can do better than that demand, since each unit above it is a unit over with no demand to meet.

```text
mincost (generic function with 1 method)
```

Example 5(d): Filling twice as slow as draining

Determine the pre-fill level if the drain rate is twice the fill rate, for the demands with and without the outlier.

The assumption in the model that is most questionable is assuming that the fill and drain rates are the same; this would only be true if the diameters of the fill and drain tubes are the same along with the flow rates being the same. If, after further investigation, it was found that the drain rate was twice the fill rate, then the model can be modified to incorporate this. Since the “cost” of filling and draining is now unbalanced, with filling taking twice as long as draining, the median point will not, in general, correspond to the optimal solution, and the cost of the pre-fill level for each part, in time, becomes

$$
\text{Pre-fill cost: } c(q, d_i) = \begin{cases} 2(d_i - q), & \text{if } d_i > q \\ q - d_i, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}
\tag{14}
$$

where

- $c(q, d_i)$ = time to fill or drain to part $i$’s volume, filling at half the rate.

The total of Eq. 14 over the parts, Eq. 13 with $c_{\text{over}} = 1$ and $c_{\text{under}} = 2$, is minimized for each data set by the implementation of Model 2:

```julia
# Code block 13: pre-fill level when filling takes twice as long
c_over, c_under = 1, 2    # time per unit drained and per unit filled
Cᵒ, qᵒ = mincost(d)       # with the demands as given
C2ᵒ, q2ᵒ = mincost(d2)    # with the outlier
qᵒ, q2ᵒ
```

```text
(237, 237)
```

At the level of 237 found with the demands as given, the 8 smaller parts are drained, 711 units in all, and the 4 larger ones filled, 465 units, so by Eq. 13 the total time is

$$
\begin{aligned}
C(237) &= c_{\text{over}} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \max\{237 - d_i, 0\} + c_{\text{under}} \sum_{i=1}^{N} \max\{d_i - 237, 0\} \\
&= 1(711) + 2(465) = 1{,}641
\end{aligned}

$$

As expected, since it is more costly to fill than to drain, the optimal pre-fill level has increased and is no longer the median but is still robust with respect to data outliers; that the level moved the way the change in costs predicts is the Nudge check of Lecture 1.2.

$q^{*} =$ 237 with the demands as given and 237 with the outlier

For a product made each day and sold at a unit price, as in Eq. 11, a unit over costs the unit cost, $c_{\text{over}} = c$, since it is made and not sold, and a unit under costs the operating unit profit, $c_{\text{under}} = p - c$, the profit of the lost sale. With perfect prediction, the number made each day exactly matches that day’s demand, so no unit is over or under, and the unit profit is earned on every unit of demand. The total operating profit over the history is then the total operating profit of perfect prediction less the overage and underage cost:

$$
\hphantom{\underset{\displaystyle \Pi^{UB}}{\Pi(q)}}\mathllap{\Pi(q)} = \mathrlap{\sum_{i=1}^{N} \Bigl[\, p \min\{q, d_i\} - c q \,\Bigr] = \Pi^{UB} - C(q)}\hphantom{\underset{\displaystyle (p - c) \sum_{i=1}^{N} d_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{N} \Bigl[\, p \min\{q, d_i\} - c q \,\Bigr] = \Pi^{UB} - C(q)}} \tag{15}
$$

$$
\hphantom{\underset{\displaystyle \Pi^{UB}}{\Pi(q)}}\mathllap{\Pi^{UB}} = \mathrlap{(p - c) \sum_{i=1}^{N} d_i}\hphantom{\underset{\displaystyle (p - c) \sum_{i=1}^{N} d_i}{\sum_{i=1}^{N} \Bigl[\, p \min\{q, d_i\} - c q \,\Bigr] = \Pi^{UB} - C(q)}} \tag{16}
$$

where

- $\Pi(q)$ = total operating profit over the history, $q$ units produced each day (\$)
- $\Pi^{UB}$ = total operating profit of perfect prediction, an upper bound on $\Pi(q)$ (\$).

so the quantity that minimizes $C(q)$ is the one that maximizes $\Pi(q)$. A salvage value or a cost of disposal, as discussed at the start of Sec. 4, changes only $c_{\text{over}}$.

Model 2 is the classic newsboy, or news vendor, problem4: each morning a newsboy buys the day’s papers before knowing how many will sell, a paper under is a sale lost, and a paper over is worth nothing the next day. The name is not used here for three reasons. It names one application, and the model serves others in which nothing is sold, the pre-fill level of Ex. 5 and, at the end of this section, the time ahead to order an item whose lead time is uncertain; one-time names what they all share, that nothing over can be carried to the next demand, which is what separates them from the periodic safety stock of Lecture 6.2. And the name comes with a way of solving the problem, the fitted distribution and its critical fractile described under Operating profit. Here, instead, the total cost of Eq. 13 is minimized on the history itself, by brute force or with an optimizer, so no distribution has to be chosen and every demand of the history is used.

Third, and most important, minimizing on the history carries over unchanged when the quantity is allowed to change from day to day with what is known that morning. Starting with the morning’s orders, and then expanding to include the website’s visitors, Ex. 6 makes them the independent variables of a multiple linear regression, Model 3, and that regression formulation is the starting point for machine learning. The basic idea is that, instead of just a point estimate, the same quantity for every demand, any additional data that is in some way correlated with the decision allows more information to be used in making it. Ex. 6 uses just two data sources, where classic machine learning techniques use dozens, if not hundreds. Machine learning is not covered in this course, but this is its starting point, and the example that follows illustrates its benefits.

Example 6: Lee Pharm’s bakery

Lee Pharm owns a bakery and has to determine each morning how many loaves of bread to bake for the day. Any loaves unsold at the end of the day are donated to the local homeless shelter. He would like some help with how to best determine the number of loaves to bake each day. He has available the number of loaves sold for each of the last 13 days:

$$
216, 214, 161, 146, 216, 159, 216, 216, 139, 216, 152, 98, 116
$$

In looking at the data, the first thing noticeable is that the number 216 appears quite often. After talking with Lee, it turns out that he typically makes 216 loaves per day, which corresponds to 18 trays of a dozen loaves. Since there was likely unmet demand any day that 216 loaves were sold, after checking with Lee, it turns out that he also has been recording the number of customers asking for bread each day after it was sold out. After adding in this unmet demand, the adjusted potential demand is:

$$
237, 214, 161, 146, 331, 159, 423, 332, 139, 327, 152, 98, 116
$$

After confirming with Lee that these past 13 days of demand are reasonably representative of typical demand, the only other information needed to provide some guidance is the average selling price of each loaf and the cost to bake each loaf, which turns out to be \$5 and \$1, respectively. Also, Lee agrees that it is reasonable to assume that any demand for a day that is not filled is lost; this is because most customers consume their bread the day of purchase, since it is made without preservatives. Determine the number of loaves to bake each day that maximizes total profit.

Example 6(a): Stationarity of the demand

Determine whether the 13 days of demand can be taken as stationary.

Before analysis, review the data for unusual values and overall patterns. Confirm questionable points with the source and remove only clear errors, not outliers by default. Also check whether the data appear stationary, since nonstationary series require detrending or other adjustments. A line plot is used because the 13 days of demand represent a time series.

Fig. 4(a) shows no trend or seasonality that would need to be accounted for in any model of the data. Most importantly, the variability does not show a long-term pattern and so it is assumed that the data is stationary. There are statistical tests for stationarity, but these would not typically be used for so few data points. Since stationarity implies the lack of trend/seasonality, the data can be randomly re-arranged (or permuted), and it should look about the same. This is done in Fig. 4(b) and (c) to verify stationarity, an Assumptions check of Lecture 1.2.

Code block 14 draws the three panels with a helper function, plotperms, so that the same check can be made on any other series by a single call. Its settings are collected at its top, and adapting the plot means changing only those. The seed of its random permutations is an optional keyword argument, 2523 unless a call gives another:

```julia
# Code block 14: a helper that plots a series as observed and in two
# random permutations, used on the bakery's demand
using Random

function plotperms(x, ylabel, caption_a; seed = 2523)
    # settings: change these to adapt the plot
    figsize = (600, 560)              # width and height, pixels
    color = bluec                     # color of the line
    arrowc = :gray40                  # color of the arrows from (a)
    sizes = (xlabelsize = 15, ylabelsize = 15,
             xticklabelsize = 13, yticklabelsize = 13)
    captions = (caption_a, "a random permutation", "a random permutation")

    # the plot: one panel per order, each captioned below
    N = length(x)                     # number of values in the series
    Random.seed!(seed)                # the same permutations every run
    orders = (1:N, randperm(N), randperm(N))
    fig = Figure(size = figsize)
    axs = [Axis(fig[2k - 1, 1]; ylabel, xticks = 1:N, sizes...)
           for k in 1:3]
    for k in 1:3
        lines!(axs[k], 1:N, x[orders[k]]; color, linewidth = 2)
        Label(fig[2k, 1], "($('a' + k - 1)) $(captions[k])";
              fontsize = 15, tellwidth = false)
    end

    # an arrow from (a) to each panel derived from it, at their right
    colsize!(fig.layout, 1, Relative(0.92))
    vp = [ax.scene.viewport[] for ax in axs]
    xr = vp[1].origin[1] + vp[1].widths[1]         # panels' right edge
    ym = [v.origin[2] + v.widths[2]/2 for v in vp] # their middles
    lines!(fig.scene, [xr + 4, xr + 22, xr + 22], [ym[1], ym[1], ym[3]];
           color = arrowc, linewidth = 1.5)
    arrows2d!(fig.scene, fill(xr + 22, 2), ym[2:3], [-18, -18], [0, 0];
              color = arrowc)
    return fig
end

d = [237, 214, 161, 146, 331, 159, 423, 332, 139, 327, 152, 98, 116]
plotperms(d, "Demand", "day by day")

```

- 1 An argument after the semicolon is a keyword argument, and one given a value, as seed is, is optional: a call that leaves it out gets 2523, and plotperms(d, "Demand", "day by day"; seed = 1) draws two other permutations.
- 2 A named tuple holds the four font sizes, so that all four are changed in one place; sizes... in the call to Axis passes each of them as a keyword argument of the same name.
- 3 The first order, 1:N, is the series as observed. randperm(N) is a random reordering of the numbers 1 to N, so indexing the series by it, as x[orders[k]] does in the call to lines!, permutes the series.
- 4 A keyword written alone, as ylabel is here and color is in the call to lines!, passes the variable of that name as the keyword argument of the same name, so the axis label is the function’s second argument.
- 5 Panel k sits in row 2k - 1 of the figure’s grid and its caption in row 2k, below it; 'a' + k - 1 is the letter a, b or c.
- 6 Once the panels are laid out, viewport gives each one’s place on the figure, in pixels from its lower left corner, so the arrows are drawn on the figure itself, fig.scene, rather than in a panel: a line from the right of (a) down to the middle of (c), with an arrowhead into (b) and into (c), the two panels derived from (a). colsize! keeps the panels to 92% of the width, leaving room for the arrows.

Figure 4: The bakery’s 13 days of demand (a) in the order observed, and (b) and (c) in two random permutations of the same values, each derived from (a), as the arrows show. The random permutations look about the same as the observed order.

The two plots of a random permutation of the demands also look stationary, lacking trend/seasonality.

The demand can be taken as stationary.

Example 6(b): Baseline and upper bound

Determine the total profit of baking 216 loaves each day, and an upper bound on total profit.

In order to be able to compare the effectiveness of any procedure, a baseline and upper bound on total profit can be determined. The baseline is the total profit associated with using the current practice of baking 216 loaves per day. An upper bound can be determined by assuming that the number of loaves baked each day exactly matches that day’s demand (perfect prediction).

Perfect prediction earns the unit profit on every unit of demand, and the total demand is the mean scaled up by the number of days, as in Lecture 1.1:

$$
\bar{d} = \frac{\sum_{i = 1}^{N} d_{i}}{N} \Rightarrow N \bar{d} = \sum_{i = 1}^{N} d_{i}

$$

With the unit price of \$5 and unit cost of \$1, the upper bound on total profit over the 13 days is then

$$
\Pi^{UB} = (p - c) \sum_{i=1}^{N} d_i = (p - c)\, N \bar{d} = (5 - 1)(2{,}835) = 11{,}340

$$

and by Eq. 15, with $c_{\text{over}} = c = 1$ and $c_{\text{under}} = p - c = 4$, baking 216 loaves every day leaves 543 loaves over on the 8 days of lower demand and 570 under on the other 5, so the baseline is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Pi(216) &= \Pi^{UB} - C(216) = 11{,}340 - \bigl[\,1(543) + 4(570)\,\bigr] \\
&= 11{,}340 - 2{,}823 = 8{,}517
\end{aligned}

$$

With the same unit price and cost, $c_{\text{over}} = c$ and $c_{\text{under}} = p - c$, and the total profit of Eq. 15, the upper bound of Eq. 16 less the total cost of Model 2’s implementation, gives the baseline:

```julia
# Code block 15: baseline and upper bound on total profit
p = 5                                # $/loaf, unit price
c = 1                                # $/loaf, unit cost
c_over = c                           # $/loaf over: baked and not sold
c_under = p - c                      # $/loaf under: the profit lost
fΠ(q, d) = (p - c)*sum(d) - fC(q, d) # total profit: bound less cost
Πᴮᴸ = fΠ(216, d)                     # baseline: 216 loaves every day
Πᵁᴮ = (p - c)*sum(d)                 # upper bound: perfect prediction
@show Πᴮᴸ
@show Πᵁᴮ
@show Πᴮᴸ/Πᵁᴮ;
```

```text
Πᴮᴸ = 8517
Πᵁᴮ = 11340
Πᴮᴸ / Πᵁᴮ = 0.7510582010582011
```

Baseline \$8,517, upper bound \$11,340, the baseline 75% of it

Example 6(c): Maximum total profit

Determine the number of loaves to bake each day that maximizes total profit, by brute force, and check it with a numerical optimizer.

Since the demand data is assumed stationary, no attempt is made to predict each day’s demand; instead, the historical demand data is taken as representative of the variability of any day’s demand, as a result, all of the data is used to determine the same (optimal) number of loaves to bake each day. Note: the numerical optimizer uses 500 as the upper bound (UB) for its search since it is likely that daily demand might exceed the maximum (423) found using just the 13 days of data.

The brute force of Model 2’s implementation evaluates the total cost of Eq. 13 at every whole number of loaves from none to the largest demand, and by Eq. 15 the least total cost is the greatest total profit:

```julia
# Code block 16: loaves that maximize total profit, by brute force
Cᵒ, qᵒ = mincost(d) # least total cost, and its loaves
Πᵒ = fΠ(qᵒ, d)      # their total profit
@show qᵒ
@show Πᵒ
@show Πᵒ/Πᵁᴮ        # share of the upper bound
@show Πᵒ/Πᴮᴸ;       # against the baseline
```

```text
qᵒ = 331
Πᵒ = 9407
Πᵒ / Πᵁᴮ = 0.8295414462081129
Πᵒ / Πᴮᴸ = 1.1044968885757895
```

and the numerical optimizer searches the interval from 0 to 500:

```julia
@show round(qᵒOptim, digits = 2)
```

The Triangulate check of Lecture 1.2 is that the brute force and the optimizer, two different methods, find the same 331 loaves (Fig. 5, the maximum in maroon). The solution recommends that Lee bake 331 loaves each morning, which should result in an over 10% increase in total profits as compared to baking only 216 loaves. The procedure works because the data is stationary, lacking trend/seasonality. If the data has a trend/seasonality, techniques exist that can try to remove the trend/seasonality so that all of the data can be used; otherwise, for non-stationary data, only the most recent data would be used in any estimate. If, for example, sales have significantly increased in the past week and are expected to remain at this higher level for at least the next few days, then the nonlinear optimization could be rerun using just the last week’s data.
